questiontext.text:
UniCV prototype for "write the expression" questions in Python. Each item is a statement in words, such as "the values a, b and c can be the sides of a triangle" or "at least one of the two people is an adult", and the student writes one Python expression for it. The expression is tested with many combinations of values and compared with the teacher's correct expression, so any expression that is equivalent is accepted (e.g. a == b == c or a == b and b == c). When an expression is wrong, the student can be shown a counterexample: values for which it gives a wrong result.

How to write a question

  1. Write the statements in the Global extra field, one block per statement:
    • ## statement: the text shown to the student. Write code between backquotes, e.g. `ano`.
    • vars: a, b, c in 0..20: the variables and their values. Possible values: integers 0..20, real numbers 0.0..10.0 (with a decimal point), a list of values "Ana", "Rui", "", or bool (True and False). Write one vars: line for each kind of variable.
    • Optional: allow: len, abs (functions that may be called: abs, len, min, max, round, int, float, str, bool, sum, sorted; by default none), forbid: not, if (operators or functions that may not be used) and require: chain (operators that must be used).
    Operators that can be named in forbid and require: and, or, not, ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, in, not in, +, -, *, /, //, %, **, if (conditional expression), chain (a chained comparison such as 0 <= x <= 10) and function names.
  2. Save (Save changes and continue editing). The statements now appear in the Answer field: write the correct expression for each one. Students do not see these expressions during the quiz (as with any question, they are shown in the review if Right answer is enabled).
  3. Keep Validate on save ticked: saving checks that every correct expression is valid. No test cases are needed.

Example of Global extra:

## The values `a`, `b` and `c` can be the sides of a triangle.
vars: a, b, c in 0..20
## The triangle with sides `a`, `b` and `c` is equilateral.
vars: a, b, c in 1..20
## At least one of the two people is an adult (18 or older).
vars: idade1, idade2 in 0..100
## The year `ano` is a leap year.
vars: ano in 1800..2400
forbid: if
## `x` is between 0 and 10, both included, written as a chained comparison.
vars: x in -5.0..15.0
require: chain

with the correct expressions a + b > c and a + c > b and b + c > a, a == b == c, idade1 >= 18 or idade2 >= 18, ano % 4 == 0 and (ano % 100 != 0 or ano % 400 == 0) and 0 <= x <= 10.

What the student gets

  • A card for each statement, with the variables and their values, the constraints (You may use, Do not use, You must use) and a box for the expression.
  • While typing, warnings for unknown names, brackets that are not closed and a single = used to compare.
  • A counter of the expressions written, a Help panel and a Start again button (with confirmation).
  • After Check, each card is marked in green or red; for a wrong expression the reason is given (e.g. "With idade1 = 0, idade2 = 18, your expression gives False, but it should give True.").

How expressions are tested

  • The student's expression and the correct expression are evaluated for many combinations of values of the variables and their results are compared, like a truth table with one row per combination; the first row where they differ is the counterexample. With bool variables it is exactly a truth table (2n rows).
  • When all the combinations are tried (see below), the check is exhaustive: within the declared values, a correct mark proves that the expression is right. Otherwise it is a well-chosen sample, very reliable but not a proof. Choose small ranges that still include the interesting cases (0..20 is enough for a triangle) to get an exhaustive check.
  • Every value of the integer ranges is tried when the number of combinations is not too large (by default up to 20000). Otherwise the values tried are the ends of the ranges, 0 and 1, the values around each number in the correct expression (for idade1 >= 18: 17, 18 and 19), multiples of those numbers (for ano % 400 == 0: 2000), random values, and combinations with equal values (for equilateral and isosceles triangles).
  • Values for which the correct expression gives an error (e.g. a division by zero) are skipped. If the correct expression gives True or False, the student's expression must give True or False too (len(nome) is not accepted for "the name is not empty").
  • Real numbers are compared with a tiny tolerance.
  • The mark is the fraction of correct expressions, unless All-or-nothing grading is ticked.
  • With Precheck enabled, the student can check that the expressions are well written (syntax, names and constraints) without testing them.

Limitations

  • An expression must fit on one line. Lambdas, assignments (:=) and comprehensions are not accepted, and methods (e.g. nome.upper()) can only be called if allow contains methods.
  • Testing many values does not prove that two expressions are equivalent: choose ranges that include the interesting cases (the borderline values are added automatically).
  • Random values can be used: choose them in Template params with Twig (e.g. {"age": {{ random(16, 21) }}}), tick Twig all, and write {{ age }} both in the statement in Global extra and in the correct expression (e.g. idade > {{ age }}).
  • Moodle's emoticon filter turns some short texts in brackets, such as the letters n, y or i between round brackets, into icons in the question text. Avoid them in the question text, or turn off the emoticon filter for the course. The statements in Global extra are shown by the interface and are not affected.

Template parameters (all optional)

  • showcounterexample (default true): if false, a wrong expression is only reported as wrong, without the values for which it fails (useful for tests).
  • maxcases (default 20000): the largest number of combinations of values tried for each statement.
  • timeout (default 10): time limit in seconds for testing all the expressions.

Example: {"showcounterexample": false}
